Step 1 · Before GitHub

Make sure you have the basics

You do not need to understand GitHub yet. Start with an account, your prepared submission files, and the hub you plan to submit to.

  • 1
    A GitHub accountYou should be able to sign in at GitHub.com. A GitHub username is not the same as your email address or display name.
  • 2
    Your prepared file or filesUse the Model Metadata Generator to create the metadata YAML for a new or updated model. Use the Data Preparation Tool to create and check the model-output file. This guide is the third tool: it shows you how those files move through GitHub.Tool 1 · MetadataTool 2 · Data preparationTool 3 · Submission guide
  • 3
    The hub you plan to submit toChoose the public forecasting, scenario, training, or sandbox hub named in your assignment or participation instructions on the next screen.
What is GitHub?
GitHub is the website many modeling hubs use to store files and review proposed changes. This guide will show you exactly where to click. It will not ask for your password or make changes for you.
Create a free GitHub account ↗
Step 2 · Destination

Which hub do you want to submit to?

A hub is a project that collects model outputs from many teams. Its files and instructions usually live in a GitHub project called a repository, or “repo.” Choose the exact hub named in your assignment or participation instructions.

CDC influenza forecasts · weekly pull-request workflow
FluSight Forecast Hub
Selecting a hub changes the repository links, example paths, warnings, and available model-output file types throughout the guide.
Copy the two-part name from the GitHub address. Example: organization/project-name.
Paste the full https:// address for the hub’s submission instructions.

Step 3 · Submission history

Have you submitted this model to this hub before?

Answer for this specific model and hub. Your answer changes the beginning of the walkthrough. It does not matter whether another model from your team has submitted before.

Choose whether this model has submitted to this hub before
Choose one answer above.
Do not use your general GitHub experience to answer. A person can be new to GitHub but still work with a returning model—or know GitHub well while submitting a new model.
Step 4 · Names

Tell the guide which account and model names to show

These values only personalize paths and examples. They stay in this browser and are not sent anywhere.

Enter the account name that appears in your GitHub profile address.
Where do I find my username?

Sign in to GitHub, select your profile picture in the upper-right corner, then select Your profile. If the address is github.com/alex-smith, the username is alex-smith. Do not enter your email address.

This identifies the forecasting model—not you or your GitHub account.
What is a model ID, and where do I find it?

A model ID is the short name used for the model’s metadata file, output folder, and forecast filename. It often looks like team-model.

Why the earlier question matters
First-time models choose a proposed ID using the hub’s current naming rules. Returning models copy the existing ID exactly. The walkthrough will show the correct route for your answer.
Open this hub’s metadata instructions ↗Search existing model IDs ↗
Only practicing? Use clearly marked sample names now; you can replace them later.
Step 5 · Forecast file

Describe the model-output file you prepared

The guide uses these two values to demonstrate the filename and folder. Use the values required by the hub, not guesses.

Format: YYYY-MM-DD. The guide starts with the Saturday that ends the current week.
What is the reference date?

The reference_date identifies the point in time from which the model output is considered to originate. It is not automatically the upload date. For weekly Saturday-based hubs, it is usually the Saturday ending the current forecast week. Always confirm the selected hub’s allowed date in its current instructions.

Only formats supported by the selected hub are shown.
How can I tell which file type I have?

Look at the end of the filename on your computer. A file ending in .csv is CSV; one ending in .parquet is Parquet. This menu changes with the selected hub, but the hub’s current instructions remain authoritative.

Need to restore the suggested date after changing it?
Check the hub’s date rules ↗

    Authoritative starting points

    Open the hub before you prepare the pull request.

    Hubverse gives repositories a shared structure, but each hub controls its own accepted rounds, formats, deadlines, and validation checks.

    Guide sources and scope

    GitHub interface images in this tutorial are current screenshots published by GitHub Docs. Repository facts and paths are linked to the public hub repositories. Screens can change, so follow button labels as well as visual placement.

    • Hubverse public hub directory
    • GitHub Docs: fork a repository
    • GitHub Docs: add a file
    • GitHub Docs: pull request from a fork
    • GitHub Desktop: commit changes
    • GitHub Docs: status checks

    About this guide

    A practice space for the GitHub submission workflow.

    This tutorial turns a public Hubverse submission into a click-by-click path for people who may be using GitHub for the first time.

    Offline version · No account access
    Purpose

    What it does

    It personalizes example repository names, file paths, branch names, and demonstrations using the setup choices made in this browser.

    Privacy

    What it does not do

    It does not sign in to GitHub, read an account, upload a file, create a branch, open a pull request, or change any repository.

    Workflow

    Where it fits

    • Prepare metadata with the Model Metadata Generator.
    • Prepare and check model output with the Data Preparation Tool.
    • Use this guide to place those prepared files on GitHub.
    • Stop when required checks pass and leave the request open for the instructor or hub team.

    Accuracy, AI-generated visuals, and scope

    Visual disclaimer: Every practice recording in this guide (GitHub website, GitHub Desktop, and command line) is an AI-generated recreation of the Windows interfaces (GitHub.com, GitHub Desktop, File Explorer, and Git Bash) rendered live in your browser from the values you entered in Setup. No real account is shown, and the live interfaces may differ in layout, counts, and dates.

    The guide links to public hub instructions for authoritative details. GitHub and hub workflows can change, so the selected hub’s current instructions and the live button labels remain authoritative.
